points.en: Twisting Scripture to serve the preacher's agenda is a kind of lying in God's name, since he speaks as though with God's words.
Manipulation: working the congregation's emotions or pressure to bypass mind and conscience and extract a response.
Using the pulpit as a weapon to attack someone who cannot answer, and plagiarism: preaching another's labor as your own.
Using other men's work is fine if done honestly and preaching is the overflow of one's own walk with God and study.
Preaching is not a performance to be admired but being gripped and set on fire by the truth, then speaking what has first gripped you.
The pulpit is not a stage: preaching for applause, reputation or effect trades a holy calling for a cheap one.
The preacher occupies the space God has given him.
Jesus forbids the world's pattern of lording it over others: 'it shall not be so among you' (Mark 10:42-43); leaders are examples, not lords.
The model is the towel and basin: Christ the King knelt to wash feet he could have commanded, so leaders first kneel and serve.
The pastor's authority is real but inverted: the authority of a servant, used for the good of those served, not the leader's comfort.
The world asks how many work for you; the Lord asks for how many you work.
James 2:1 forbids holding the faith of Christ with partiality or favoritism, because God shows none.
Impartiality means the same standard, patience and grace for rich and poor, friend and foe, influential and inconvenient alike.
Example: the pastor who fawns over the wealthy donor and overlooks the poor widow, or bends rules for friends.
First step: a private word with the brother alone, aiming to win him.
If he will not hear, take one or two others as witnesses; if still refused, tell the church.
Only if he refuses even the church is he treated as an outsider.
The escalation is patient: each stage gives room for repentance and widens the circle only as far as his hardness requires.
First purpose, always the goal: restoration of the sinning brother.
Second: the purity of the church, so a little leaven does not corrupt the whole lump.
Third: the honor of Christ's name before a watching world.
Discipline is misused when leaders skip the private steps for public exposure, act from wounded pride or anger, or use it to silence critics or crush people.
Discipline that has lost the goal of restoration has ceased to be biblical discipline.
Galatians 6:1 requires restoring in a spirit of gentleness, considering yourself lest you also be tempted.
Gossip is among the chief solvents of Christian unity; a congregation given to it is eaten hollow from within while professing love.
It is dangerous because it feels small and natural and is disguised as concern or a prayer request, so its harm goes unrecognized.
Scripture treats the tongue seriously: James calls it a fire, and a whisperer separates close friends (Proverbs 16:28).
The pastor must refuse to traffic in gossip himself, neither repeating what he need not nor being its source or eager hearer.
He must also courageously confront gossip in the flock, gently stopping it and teaching his people to do the same.
A man cannot lead a pure-tongued church while indulging an impure tongue in private.
The difference is not the subject matter, since both may concern another's fault, but direction, motive and goal.
Biblical confrontation goes to the person or through the Matthew 18 channels; gossip talks about him to those who are neither problem nor solution.
Confrontation aims at the offender's restoration; gossip aims to wound, vent, or lift the teller by lowering the subject.
